title: 1 Kings 8:1–11
context: With the temple complete, Solomon gathers Israel’s elders and the whole nation in the seventh month, Ethanim, to bring the ark of the covenant up from the City of David to the new house. The priests carry the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and the holy vessels, while the king and people offer sacrifices beyond counting. The ark, containing only the two stone tablets from Horeb, is set in the most holy place under the cherubim’s wings. When the priests come out, the cloud of the LORD’s glory fills the house so that they cannot stand to minister, recalling the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34–35. The parallel account is 2 Chronicles 5:2–14. Earlier in the book, 6:38 dates the temple’s completion to the eighth month; the text does not say how much time passed before this dedication.

verses.text: Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel with all the heads of the tribes, the princes of the fathers’ households of the children of Israel, to King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the LORD’s covenant out of David’s city, which is Zion.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon gathers the elders and tribal leaders to bring the ark up from the City of David. Arminian readers note that the king involves the whole leadership of Israel, making the dedication a shared act of the covenant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ark’s journey to the temple as the climax of a movement that began with David bringing it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as a covenant celebration centered on the LORD’s presence.

verses.text: All the men of Israel assembled themselves to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel assembles at the feast in the seventh month, Ethanim. Arminian readers note that the timing places the dedication within Israel’s calendar of worship; many link it to the autumn feast of booths, though the text names only the month.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the timing a joining of the temple’s dedication to Israel’s remembrance of God’s past provision. Both traditions acknowledge that the name Ethanim is explained in the verse itself as the seventh month, and avoid going beyond that.

verses.text: All the elders of Israel came, and the priests picked up the ark.
verses.arminianNotes: The elders come and the priests pick up the ark. Arminian readers note that the priests carry it properly, a contrast with the earlier mishandling that led to Uzzah’s death in 2 Samuel 6:6–7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the care taken as reverence for God’s holiness, which requires that His worship follow His instruction. Shared ground: both traditions read the priests’ role as faithful obedience to the pattern God had given for moving the ark.

verses.text: They brought up the LORD’s ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the Tent. The priests and the Levites brought these up.
verses.arminianNotes: The ark, the Tent of Meeting, and the holy vessels are brought up by the priests and Levites. Arminian readers note that the older wilderness sanctuary is brought into the new house, showing continuity with Israel’s earlier worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the temple as fulfilling, not replacing, what the tabernacle signified. Both traditions acknowledge that the text does not say where the Tent of Meeting had been kept; some connect it with Gibeon (compare 2 Chronicles 1:3), but this is not stated here.

verses.text: King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who were assembled to him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle that could not be counted or numbered for multitude.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon and the congregation offer sheep and cattle beyond counting before the ark. Arminian readers see joyful, wholehearted worship from the whole people, gathered with their king before the LORD’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abundance of sacrifices as fitting gratitude for God’s faithfulness to His covenant. Shared ground: both traditions read the uncounted offerings as an expression of worship, not as payment for God’s favor.

verses.text: The priests brought in the ark of the LORD’s covenant to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, to the most holy place, even under the cherubim’s wings.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests bring the ark into the most holy place under the cherubim’s wings. Arminian readers note that the ark is described as reaching “its place,” a sense of arrival after long years of movement since the wilderness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inner sanctuary as the place where God’s throne is pictured among His people, with the cherubim over the ark. Both traditions read the verse as the center of the dedication: the covenant ark set in the house built for the LORD’s name.

verses.text: For the cherubim spread their wings out over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles above.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim’s wings spread over the ark and its poles. Arminian readers note the careful description, which draws attention to the holiness of the place and the guarding of the covenant within it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cherubim as signs of God’s heavenly throne, recalling the cherubim on the ark’s cover in Exodus 25:18–22. Shared ground: both traditions read the detail as pointing to God’s holy presence, without forcing further symbolism.

verses.text: The poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the holy place before the inner sanctuary, but they were not seen outside. They are there to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: The poles are long enough to be seen from the holy place but not outside, and the narrator says they are there to this day. Arminian readers note that the phrase suggests a source written while the temple still stood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the poles’ visibility as a quiet reminder that the ark was once carried through the wilderness. Both traditions treat “to this day” as the narrator’s or source’s perspective, without claiming more about how the book was compiled.

verses.text: There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets which Moses put there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the children of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Only the two stone tablets from Horeb are in the ark. Arminian readers see the covenant law at the heart of Israel’s worship, placing obedience to God’s word at the center of the temple’s meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the tablets as the covenant document, showing that the temple rests on God’s prior grace in bringing Israel out of Egypt. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking the temple to Sinai, and note Hebrews 9:4 by reference as a related text.

verses.text: It came to pass, when the priests had come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled the LORD’s house,
verses.arminianNotes: When the priests leave the holy place, the cloud fills the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see God graciously answering the people’s worship by manifesting His presence among them in a visible way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cloud as God’s sovereign choice to dwell among His people, as He did at the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). Shared ground: both traditions read the cloud as a sign of the LORD’s real presence and approval of the house.

verses.text: so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for the LORD’s glory filled the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests cannot stand to minister because the LORD’s glory fills the house. Arminian readers note that human service gives way before God’s glory, which overwhelms even those appointed to minister.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as echoing Exodus 40:35, where Moses could not enter the tent. Shared ground: both traditions treat the glory filling the house as fully agreed, and neither draws a contrast from it; it marks God taking up residence.
